Memorandum 
To:   Business & Economic Development Committee 
From: Planning Division 
Date:   October 5, 2026 
Regarding: Floor area ratio (FAR) removal from the Downtown Development District (DDD) 
This memo outlines the proposed removal of the floor area ratio (FAR) from the Downtown Development 
District (DDD). A need has been expressed to create more flexibility for expanding businesses and residences 
downtown. The floor area ratio in Downtown Development District can hinder infill development. Once the 
maximum floor area ratio is met on a lot, no additional floor area may be added.  
Floor area ratio is the floor area of a building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot. A building with 
40,000 sqft of floor area on a 10,000 square foot lot has a FAR of 4.0. A building with 10,000sqft of floor area 
on a 40,000sqft lot has a FAR of 0.25.  
Floor area ratio (FAR) is an outdated control; originally, it was placed in the code to address the following 
planning objectives:   
 Control development intensity – limiting how much building floor area there could be on a lot without 
simply dictating a particular building footprint. 
 Managing building scale – FAR is often used to limit the bulk of a building 
 Allowing flexibility in design – unlike a simple lot coverage requirement, a developer can choose 
between a shorter, wider building or a taller narrower one 
 Separating out core, more dense allowances to less density. 
FAR is not used as much in modern zoning because:  
 FAR doesn’t directly control building form – a FAR number can produce many different buildings so if 
the city cares about other elements like frontage, setbacks, streetscape, public space, FAR will not 
address those priorities. 
 Modern zoning often focuses on form rather than intensity such as building to street relationship and 
massing in a downtown 
 In the downtown, FAR could have unintended consequences.  If the city wants to have a certain 
number of stories in a building to create mass and pedestrian scale, FAR will not provide that form. 
 FAR is difficult to understand – other requirements like minimums and maximums are easier to explain. 
 FAR can discourage infill development or in the case that brought us here for this discussion, the 
addition of stories to an important building. 
 FAR does not necessarily protect sunlight or neighborhood character because it does not consider how 
buildings are designed or positioned and the heights of them.  
 Floor area is not a good measure to ensure infrastructure capacity. A multi-unit residential development 
and commercial development both with 40,000sqft of floor area will have different levels of usage and 
impacts on infrastructure. The City also has to ensure that all developments have adequate 
infrastructure capacity through other standards in the Ordinance.
City of Bangor Department of Community & Economic Development – Planning Division 
 
 
Thus, rather than asking What FAR should this district have, we would ask what form, intensity, capacity 
and relationship to the street does this building have in our downtown? 
For these reasons, staff will be recommending removal of this control in the new Land Development Code. 
However, this current proposed text amendment will only remove it from the Downtown Development District 
(DDD) since new development is proposed there that would be limited by this. 
Additionally, some of the most well-known historic buildings downtown already exceed this standard. For 
example, the Graham Building where the Rudman Winchell offices are has a FAR of approximately 4.5 and the 
Eastern Trust building at 6 State Street has a FAR of about 5.3. 
The proposed amendment aligns with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply downtown by 
revising zoning regulations. 
The proposed language is included in your packets and will also be on the October 6th Planning Board agenda 
for the Board’s feedback. If Councilors and Planning Board are amenable, staff will forward the formal 
language through for adoption.

Title, Ordinance 
 
Amending Chapter 165, Land Development, Attachment 2 - Schedule A, Urban Developed Area to Remove 
Floor Area Ratio (FAR) from the Downtown Development District (DDD) 
 
Summary 
 
This amendment would remove Floor Area Ratio (FAR) from the Downtown Development District (DDD) to 
provide flexibility for growth in downtown and promote infill development. Floor area ratio is the floor area of a 
building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot. 
 
FAR was used to control building bulk and volume in the early to mid-20th century. When FARs were 
implemented around the country, some of the perceived benefits were protecting sunlight, neighborhood 
character, and infrastructure capacity, most of which do not hold true today. Additionally, some of the most 
well-known historic buildings downtown already exceed this standard. For example, the Graham Building 
where the Rudman Winchell offices are has a FAR of approximately 4.5 and the Eastern Trust building at 6 
State Street has a FAR of about 5.3. 
 
The proposed amendments align with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply downtown by 
revising zoning regulations.

Memorandum 
To:   Business & Economic Development Committee 
From: Planning Division 
Date:   September 22, 2026 
Regarding: Proposed new fees 
The purpose of this memo is to discuss potential new fees to cover costs incurred for land development 
projects, zoning map changes, and historic preservation applications. Currently, there is no fee to send mailed 
notices for these applications. However, notices to abutting property owners are required for almost all types of 
development, all zoning map changes, and historic preservation applications. Depending on whether the 
project is a conditional use or there are many abutting property owners, mailings can be quite large. Due to the 
number of development projects, zone change requests, and historic preservation applications, the number of 
mailed notices that go out every year can be substantial. Therefore, similar to how the City charges developers 
for the cost to advertise certain developments and review land development permits, staff proposes to charge 
for the cost to mail notices to abutters so that this cost doesn’t fall on taxpayers. The cost to print and mail a 
letter is roughly $1.09-1.35 per letter, $0.31-0.57 of which is for the printing and envelope and $0.78 of which is 
for the postage. We would propose charging in the middle of this range at $1.22/letter. Since postage is paid 
for from Treasury, the amount that would be reimbursed to the C&ED Department for postage would be 
transferred to Treasury. 
Another proposed new fee is to cover the cost of stormwater permitting review. Recently, the City was given 
delegated authority by the State to review the stormwater permits triggered by developments that create 
20,000 square feet of new impervious area within an urban impaired stream watershed or one acre of 
impervious area in unimpaired watersheds. However, this authority comes with extra staff time needed to 
review projects and inspect stormwater systems to ensure compliance. The State currently charges developers 
for this permitting; therefore, staff are proposing to charge a similar amount for the City to do this permitting. 
This fee would be charged as part of the land development permit application for a project (if it meets the 
threshold for requiring this permitting), and the stormwater permitting portion would be transferred to the 
Stormwater Utility fund to cover these extra costs. This fee would not apply to sites with stormwater permits 
previously issued by Maine DEP; revisions to those permits would have to be completed by Maine DEP.

Memorandum 
To:   Business & Economic Development Committee 
From: Planning Division 
Date:   September 29, 2026 
Regarding: Proposed climate rebate program for residents 
The purpose of this memo is to discuss a proposed new climate rebate program for residents of the City that 
would be focused on saving households money on energy bills. Details have not been worked out yet (they 
would be established over the next month or so), but the program would allocate up to $50,000 from the 
Climate Action Plan funds to provide rebates to residents for weatherization, heat pump installations, and 
possibly solar. This would work in concert with rebates provided by Efficiency Maine and the City’s CDBG 
program by providing “gap financing” (covering any funding gap leftover by these other rebate programs). 
Climate Action Plan funds are intended for actions that help implement the Penobscot Climate Action Plan. 
This program would implement Toolkit 21 in the Climate Action Plan, which recommends helping residents with 
retrofitting their homes. This was one of the highest impact toolkits in the plan, having a very high potential to 
reduce greenhouse gas emissions and high potential to build community resilience. It has the added benefit of 
saving households money during a very expensive heating season. 
Initial public outreach at the Farmers’ market on a potential program like this garnered a lot of excitement. Staff 
gave people the option to choose a category that would help their household the most - weatherization, solar, 
bikes, and an “other options” category. People who gave feedback were evenly split between the different 
categories, so staff would propose providing rebates for different options since these would serve different 
needs (heat pumps would help households that currently use heating oil to save the most money, while solar 
would help households that use electric heating save the most, and weatherization would help all households 
save money). The benefit of all three of these categories would be that they would save households money 
over many heating (and cooling) seasons. Given the high price of heating oil and the efficiency difference 
between heat pumps and oil heating, it may make the best use of funds to limit any heat pump rebates to 
residents currently using oil. Also, similar to Efficiency Maine, staff would propose tiering the rebate amount 
based on income, so lower income residents would receive a higher rebate. Staff would also propose that an 
energy audit be completed and funded by this program first before weatherization and heat pumps are done in 
order to help identify the best strategy for each home (such as whether weatherization needs to be done 
before a heat pump is installed).
